arXiv:1805.02775v2 [math.CA] 19 Jun 2018

Sharp L2L^{2} estimate of Schrödinger maximal function in higher dimensions

Xiumin Du Address:  Institute for Advanced Study
Princeton, NJ Email address: xdu@math.ias.edu and Ruixiang Zhang Address:  Institute for Advanced Study
Princeton, NJ Email address: rzhang@math.ias.edu Dedicated to Jean Bourgain with admiration
Abstract.

We show that, for n≥3n\geq 3, limt→0ei​t​Δ​f​(x)=f⁡(x)\lim_{t\to 0}e^{it\Delta}f(x)=f(x) holds almost everywhere for all f∈Hs​(ℝn)f\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) provided that s>n2​(n+1)s>\frac{n}{2(n+1)}. Due to a counterexample by Bourgain, up to the endpoint, this result is sharp and fully resolves a problem raised by Carleson. Our main theorem is a fractal L2L^{2} restriction estimate, which also gives improved results on the size of divergence set of Schrödinger solutions, the Falconer distance set problem and the spherical average Fourier decay rates of fractal measures. The key ingredients of the proof include multilinear Kakeya estimates, decoupling and induction on scales.

1. Introduction

The solution to the free Schrödinger equation

(1.1) {i​ut−Δ​u=0,(x,t)∈ℝn×ℝu⁡(x,0)=f⁡(x),x∈ℝn\begin{cases}iu_{t}-\Delta u=0,&(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}\\ u(x,0)=f(x),&x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\end{cases}

is given by

ei​t​Δ​f​(x)=(2​π)−n​∫ei⁡(x⋅ξ+t​|ξ|2)​f^​(ξ)​𝑑ξ.e^{it\Delta}f(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{i\left(x\cdot\xi+t|\xi|^{2}\right)}\widehat{f}(\xi)\,d\xi.

In [8], Carleson proposed the problem of identifying the optimal ss for which limt→0ei​t​Δ​f​(x)=f⁡(x)\lim_{t\to 0}e^{it\Delta}f(x)=f(x) almost everywhere whenever f∈Hs​(ℝn),f\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), and proved convergence for s≥14s\geq\frac{1}{4} when n=1n=1. Dahlberg and Kenig [10] then showed that this result is sharp. The higher dimensional case has since been studied by several authors [7, 9, 28, 30, 2, 26, 29, 20, 3, 23, 11, 4, 24, 12, 13]. In particular, almost everywhere convergence holds if s>12−14​ns>\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4n} when n≥2n\geq 2 (n=2n=2 due to Lee [20] and n≥2n\geq 2 due to Bourgain [3]). Recently Bourgain [4] gave counterexamples showing that convergence can fail if s<n2​(n+1)s<\frac{n}{2(n+1)}. Since then, Guth, Li and the first author [12] improved the sufficient condition when n=2n=2 to the almost sharp range s>13s>\frac{1}{3}. In higher dimensions (n≥3n\geq 3), Guth, Li and the authors [13] proved the convergence for s>n+12​(n+2)s>\frac{n+1}{2(n+2)}.

In this article, we establish the following theorem, which is sharp up to the endpoint.

Theorem 1.1.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. For every f∈Hs​(ℝn)f\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) with s>n2​(n+1)s>\frac{n}{2(n+1)}, limt→0ei​t​Δ​f​(x)=f⁡(x)\lim_{t\to 0}e^{it\Delta}f(x)=f(x) almost everywhere.

We use Bm​(x,r)B^{m}(x,r) to represent a ball centered at xx with radius rr in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}. By a standard smooth approximation argument, Theorem 1.1 is a consequence of the following estimate of Schrödinger maximal function:

Theorem 1.2.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. For any s>n2​(n+1)s>\frac{n}{2(n+1)}, the following bound holds: for any function f∈Hs​(ℝn)f\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),

(1.2) ‖sup0<t≤1|ei​t​Δ​f|‖L2​(Bn​(0,1))≤Cs​‖f‖Hs​(ℝn).\left\|\sup_{0<t\leq 1}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}(B^{n}(0,1))}\leq C_{s}\|f\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}.

Via a localization argument, Littlewood-Paley decomposition and parabolic rescaling, Theorem 1.2 is reduced to the following theorem which we will prove in this paper:

Theorem 1.3.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists a constant CϵC_{\epsilon} such that

(1.3) ‖sup0<t≤R​|ei​t​Δ​f|‖L2​(Bn​(0,R))≤Cϵ​Rn2​(n+1)+ε​‖f‖2\left\|\underset{0<t\leq R}{\text{sup}}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}(B^{n}(0,R))}\leq C_{\epsilon}R^{\frac{n}{2(n+1)}+\varepsilon}\|f\|_{2}

holds for all R≥1R\geq 1 and all ff with supp​f^⊂A⁡(1)={ξ∈ℝn:|ξ|∼1}{\rm supp}\widehat{f}\subset A(1)=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|\xi|\sim 1\}.

Remark 1.4.

Our results above are new in the case n≥3n\geq 3. When n=1,2n=1,2, despite the fact that we recover the almost sharp results of pointwise convergence problem, our sharp L2L^{2} estimates of Schrödinger maximal function are not as strong as the previous sharp LpL^{p} estimates:

(1.4) ‖supt>0|ei​t​Δ​f|‖L4​(ℝ)≤C​‖f‖H1/4​(ℝ),[19, Kenig-Ponce-Vega],\left\|\sup_{t>0}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{R})}\leq C\|f\|_{H^{1/4}(\mathbb{R})}\,,\quad\text{\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{KPV}{}{}, Kenig-Ponce-Vega]}}\,,

and

(1.5) ‖sup0<t≤1|ei​t​Δf|‖L3​(ℝ2)≤Cs∥f∥Hs​(ℝ2),∀s>13,[12, D.-Guth-Li].\left\|\sup_{0<t\leq 1}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq C_{s}\|f\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\,,\forall s>\frac{1}{3},\quad\text{\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{DGL}{}{}, D.-Guth-Li]}}\,.

From the same examples as what one has for the restriction conjecture, it seems reasonable to have a similar conjecture in higher dimensions - it would be interesting to ask if the following holds for general nn:

(1.6) ‖sup0<t≤1|ei​t​Δ​f|‖L2​(n+1)n​(ℝn)≤C​‖f‖Hn2​(n+1)​(ℝn).\left\|\sup_{0<t\leq 1}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{\frac{2(n+1)}{n}}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C\|f\|_{H^{\frac{n}{2(n+1)}}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\,.

From (1.4) and (1.5) we see that (1.6) is true for n=1n=1, and is true up to the endpoint for n=2n=2. However, the estimate (1.6) fails in higher dimensions. During the MRC week in June 2018, Jongchon Kim, Hong Wang and the authors worked together on the following local estimates:

(1.7) ‖sup0<t≤1|ei​t​Δ​f|‖Lp​(Bn​(0,1))≤Cs​‖f‖Hs​(ℝn),∀s>n2​(n+1),\left\|\sup_{0<t\leq 1}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{p}(B^{n}(0,1))}\leq C_{s}\|f\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\,,\forall s>\frac{n}{2(n+1)}\,,

and by looking at Bourgain’s counterexample [4] in every intermediate dimension, the working group observed that (1.7) fails if p>p0:=2+4(n−1)​(n+2)p>p_{0}:=2+\frac{4}{(n-1)(n+2)}. Note that 2​(n+1)n>p0\frac{2(n+1)}{n}>p_{0} when n≥3n\geq 3 and henceforth (1.6) fails. To our best knowledge, the following two problems are still open when n≥3n\geq 3: determine the optimal p=p⁡(n)p=p(n) for which we can have (1.7) and identify the optimal s=s⁡(n,p)s=s(n,p) for which (1.7) with p>2p>2 fixed holds. Our working group at MRC had some partial results and planned to deal with these problems in an upcoming paper.

Our main result is the following fractal L2L^{2} restriction estimate, from which Theorem 1.3 follows.

Theorem 1.5.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists constant CεC_{\varepsilon} such that the following holds for all R≥1R\geq 1 and all ff with supp​f^⊂Bn​(0,1){\rm supp}\widehat{f}\subset B^{n}(0,1). Suppose that X=⋃kBkX=\bigcup_{k}B_{k} is a union of lattice unit cubes in Bn+1​(0,R)B^{n+1}(0,R) and each lattice R1/2R^{1/2}-cube intersecting XX contains ∼λ\sim\lambda many unit cubes in XX. Let 1≤α≤n+11\leq\alpha\leq n+1 and γ\gamma be given by

(1.8) γ:=maxBn+1​(x′,r)⊂Bn+1​(0,R)x′∈ℝn+1,r≥1#⁡{Bk:Bk⊂B⁡(x′,r)}rα.\gamma:=\max_{\underset{x^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1},r\geq 1}{B^{n+1}(x^{\prime},r)\subset B^{n+1}(0,R)}}\frac{\#\{B_{k}:B_{k}\subset B(x^{\prime},r)\}}{r^{\alpha}}\,.

Then

(1.9) ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X)≤Cε​γ2(n+1)​(n+2)​λn(n+1)​(n+2)​Rα(n+1)​(n+2)+ε​‖f‖2.\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)}\leq C_{\varepsilon}\gamma^{\frac{2}{(n+1)(n+2)}}\lambda^{\frac{n}{(n+1)(n+2)}}R^{\frac{\alpha}{(n+1)(n+2)}+\varepsilon}\|f\|_{2}\,.

Note that in Theorem 1.5, λ≤γ​Rα/2\lambda\leq\gamma R^{\alpha/2}. As a direct result of Theorem 1.5, there holds a slightly weaker fractal L2L^{2} restriction estimate. It has a relatively simpler statement:

Corollary 1.6.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists constant CεC_{\varepsilon} such that the following holds for all R≥1R\geq 1 and all ff with supp​f^⊂Bn​(0,1){\rm supp}\widehat{f}\subset B^{n}(0,1). Suppose that X=⋃kBkX=\bigcup_{k}B_{k} is a union of lattice unit cubes in Bn+1​(0,R)B^{n+1}(0,R). Let 1≤α≤n+11\leq\alpha\leq n+1 and γ\gamma be given by

(1.10) γ:=maxBn+1​(x′,r)⊂Bn+1​(0,R)x′∈ℝn+1,r≥1#⁡{Bk:Bk⊂B⁡(x′,r)}rα.\gamma:=\max_{\underset{x^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1},r\geq 1}{B^{n+1}(x^{\prime},r)\subset B^{n+1}(0,R)}}\frac{\#\{B_{k}:B_{k}\subset B(x^{\prime},r)\}}{r^{\alpha}}\,.

Then

(1.11) ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X)≤Cε​γ1n+1​Rα2​(n+1)+ε​‖f‖2.\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)}\leq C_{\varepsilon}\gamma^{\frac{1}{n+1}}R^{\frac{\alpha}{2(n+1)}+\varepsilon}\|f\|_{2}\,.

We will see that Corollary 1.6 is sufficient to derive the sharp L2L^{2} estimate of Schrödinger maximal function (Theorem 1.3) and all other applications in Section 2. This corollary can also be proved directly by a slightly simpler argument. The case n=1n=1 of Corollary 1.6 can be recovered using the ingredients in Wolff’s paper [31]. See Subsection 3.3 for a discussion.

Nevertheless, Theorem 1.5 has two advantages compared to Corollary 1.6. Firstly, it gives us a better L2L^{2} restriction estimate if the set XX of unit cubes is fairly sparse. Secondly, it tells us some geometric information about a set XX of unit cubes when ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X)\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)} is comparable to ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(B​(0,R))\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(B(0,R))}. For example, taking α=n+1\alpha=n+1 (hence γ≲1\gamma\lesssim 1) we have:

Corollary 1.7.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. Suppose that X=⋃kBkX=\bigcup_{k}B_{k} is a union of lattice unit cubes in Bn+1​(0,R)B^{n+1}(0,R) and each lattice R1/2R^{1/2}-cube intersecting XX contains ∼λ\sim\lambda many unit cubes in XX. Suppose there is a function ff with supp​f^⊂Bn​(0,1){\rm supp}\widehat{f}\subset B^{n}(0,1) and ‖f‖2≠0\|f\|_{2}\neq 0 such that ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X)≳R1/2​‖f‖2\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)}\gtrsim R^{1/2}\|f\|_{2}. Then λ⪆Rn+12\lambda\gtrapprox R^{\frac{n+1}{2}}.

As a remark, the scale R1/2R^{1/2} in Corollary 1.7 is the largest one can have. Indeed, with the assumption of the corollary, the unit cubes in XX do not have to almost fill RβR^{\beta}-cubes completely for β>1/2\beta>1/2. One can see this from the Knapp example where we only have one wave packet.

To prove our main result - Theorem 1.5, we will use a broad-narrow analysis, which has similar spirit as the techniques in the work of Bourgain-Guth [6], Bourgain [3], Bourgain-Demeter [5] and Guth [18].

In the broad case, we can exploit the transversality and apply the multilinear refined Strichartz estimate, which is a result obtained by Guth, Li and the authors in [13] (see [12, 14, 13] for applications of refined Strichartz estimate). In the narrow case, we use the l2l^{2} decoupling theorem of Bourgain-Demeter [5] in a lower dimension and perform induction on scales. The way we do induction has its roots in the proof of the linear refined Strichartz estimate, due to Guth, Li and the first author (essentially proved in [12], see [13] for the statement in general setting).

Our method is related to Bourgain’s in [3]. In [3], Bourgain had a similar broad-narrow analysis (we have here the size of the small ball being K2K^{2} instead of KK as in [3] for a technical issue similar to what one has in [5, 18]). He then applied multilinear restriction to control the broad part in the sharp range s>n2​(n+1)s>\frac{n}{2(n+1)} (except the endpoint). He speculated from this that the above range of ss might be sharp (see the end of the introduction in [4]). In [3] the narrow part was handled following the general approach from [6], which gives non-sharp estimates. Historically, one could view the present non-endpoint solution to Carleson’s problem as building on [3], providing a subtler way of handling the narrow part and proving Corollary 1.6. For the stronger Theorem 1.5 and Corollary 1.7, one needs a different ingredient, namely the multilinear refined Strichartz in [13], to handle the broad part.

In Section 2 we show how Corollary 1.6 and Theorem 1.3 follow from Theorem 1.5, and we also present applications of Theorem 1.5 to other problems - bounding the size of divergence set of Schrödinger solutions (Theorem 2.4), the Falconer distance set problem (Theorem 2.6 and 2.7) and the spherical average Fourier decay rates of fractal measures (Theorem 2.8). We prove Theorem 1.5 in Section 3.

2. Applications of Theorem 1.5

2.1. Sharp L2L^{2} estimate of Schrödinger maximal function

In this subsection, we show how Corollary 1.6 and Theorem 1.3 follow from Theorem 1.5, via dyadic pigeonholing argument and locally constant property.

Proof of (Theorem 1.5 ⟹\implies Corollary 1.6).

Given X=⋃kBkX=\bigcup_{k}B_{k}, a union of lattice unit cubes in Bn+1​(0,R)B^{n+1}(0,R) satisfying the assumptions of Corollary 1.6, we sort the lattice R1/2R^{1/2}-cubes in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1} intersecting XX by the number λ\lambda of unit cubes BkB_{k} contained in it. Since 1≤λ≤RO⁡(1)1\leq\lambda\leq R^{O(1)}, there are only O⁡(log⁡R)O(\log R) choices for dyadic number λ\lambda. So we can choose a dyadic number λ\lambda and a subset ℬλ\mathcal{B}_{\lambda} of {Bk}\{B_{k}\} such that for each unit cube BB in ℬλ\mathcal{B}_{\lambda}, the lattice R1/2R^{1/2}-cube containing it contains ∼λ\sim\lambda many unit cubes from ℬλ\mathcal{B}_{\lambda} and

‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X)⪅‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(⋃B∈ℬλB).\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)}\lessapprox\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}_{\lambda}}B)}\,.

By applying Theorem 1.5 to ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(⋃B∈ℬλB)\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}_{\lambda}}B)}, we get

‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X)⪅γ2(n+1)​(n+2)​λn(n+1)​(n+2)​Rα(n+1)​(n+2)​‖f‖2,\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)}\lessapprox\gamma^{\frac{2}{(n+1)(n+2)}}\lambda^{\frac{n}{(n+1)(n+2)}}R^{\frac{\alpha}{(n+1)(n+2)}}\|f\|_{2}\,,

and (1.11) follows from the fact that λ≤γ​Rα/2\lambda\leq\gamma R^{\alpha/2}. ∎

Proof of (the case α=n\alpha=n of Corollary 1.6 ⟹\implies Theorem 1.3).

We aim to show that

(2.1) ‖sup0<t<R|ei​t​Δ​f|‖L2​(Bn​(0,R))⪅Rn2​(n+1)​‖f‖2\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}(B^{n}(0,R))}\lessapprox R^{\frac{n}{2(n+1)}}\|f\|_{2}

holds for all R≥1R\geq 1 and all ff with Fourier support in A⁡(1):={ξ∈ℝn:|ξ|∼1}A(1):=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|\xi|\sim 1\}.

By viewing |ei​t​Δ​f​(x)||e^{it\Delta}f(x)| essentially as constant on unit balls22 2 We refer the readers to [6, Sections 2-5] for the standard formalism of this locally constant property., we can find a set XX described as follows: XX is a union of unit balls in Bn​(0,R)×[0,R]B^{n}(0,R)\times[0,R] satisfying that each vertical thin tube of dimensions 1×⋯×1×R1\times\cdots\times 1\times R contains exactly one unit ball in XX, and

(2.2) ‖sup0<t<R|ei​t​Δ​f|‖L2​(Bn​(0,R))⪅‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X).\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}(B^{n}(0,R))}\lessapprox\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)}\,.

The desired estimate (2.1) follows by applying Corollary 1.6 to ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(X)\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{2}(X)} with α=n\alpha=n and γ≲1\gamma\lesssim 1. ∎

By formalizing the locally constant property, from Corollary 1.6 we derive some weighted L2L^{2} estimates - Theorem 2.2 and 2.3, which in turn have applications on several problems described below.

(2.3) μ⁡(B⁡(x,r))≤Cμ​rα,∀r>0,∀x∈ℝd.\mu(B(x,r))\leq C_{\mu}r^{\alpha},\quad\forall r>0,\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Let n≥1,α∈(0,n]n\geq 1,\alpha\in(0,n] and μ\mu be an α\alpha-dimensional measure in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then

(2.4) ‖sup0<t<R|ei​t​Δ​f|‖L2​(Bn​(0,R),d​μR​(x))⪅Rα2​(n+1)​‖f‖2,\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n}(0,R);d\mu_{R}(x)\right)}\lessapprox R^{\frac{\alpha}{2(n+1)}}\|f\|_{2}\,,

whenever R≥1R\geq 1 and ff has Fourier support in Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1).

Theorem 2.3.

Let n≥1,α∈(0,n+1]n\geq 1,\alpha\in(0,n+1] and μ\mu be an α\alpha-dimensional measure in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. Then

(2.5) ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖L2​(Bn+1​(0,R),d​μR​(x,t))⪅Rα2​(n+1)​‖f‖2,\left\|e^{it\Delta}f\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n+1}(0,R);d\mu_{R}(x,t)\right)}\lessapprox R^{\frac{\alpha}{2(n+1)}}\|f\|_{2}\,,

Theorem 2.2 and 2.3 are new when n≥2,α∈(2,3)n\geq 2,\alpha\in(2,3) or n≥3,α∈(n+12,n+1)n\geq 3,\alpha\in(\frac{n+1}{2},n+1) (c.f. [14, 22]). We defer the proof of these weighted L2L^{2} estimates to the end of this subsection. Let’s first see their applications. We omit history and various previous results on the following three problems and refer the readers to [13, 14, 22] and the references therein.

(I) Hausdorff dimension of divergence set of Schrödinger solutions

A natural refinement of Carleson’s problem was initiated by Sjögren and Sjölin [27]: determine the size of divergence set, in particular, consider

αn​(s):=supf∈Hs​(ℝn)dim⁡{x∈ℝn:limt→0ei​t​Δ​f​(x)≠f⁡(x)},\alpha_{n}(s):=\sup_{f\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}{\rm dim}\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\lim_{t\to 0}e^{it\Delta}f(x)\neq f(x)\right\}\,,

where dim{\rm dim} stands for the Hausdorff dimension.

The following theorem is a direct result of Theorem 2.2 (c.f. [13, 22]). When n=2n=2, it recovers the corresponding result derived from the sharp L3L^{3} estimate of Schrödinger maximal function in D.-Guth-Li [12]. When n≥3n\geq 3, it improves the previous best known result in D.-Guth-Li-Z. [13].

Theorem 2.4.

Let n≥2n\geq 2. Then

(2.6) αn​(s)≤n+1−2​(n+1)​sn,n2​(n+1)<s<n4.\alpha_{n}(s)\leq n+1-\frac{2(n+1)s}{n},\quad\frac{n}{2(n+1)}<s<\frac{n}{4}\,.

(II) Falconer distance set problem

Let E⊂ℝdE\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact subset, its distance set Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E) is defined by

Δ(E):={|x−y|:x,y∈E}.\Delta(E):=\{|x-y|:x,y\in E\}\,.
Conjecture 2.5 (Falconer [15]).

Let d≥2d\geq 2 and E⊂ℝdE\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set. Then

dim⁡(E)>d2⇒|Δ⁡(E)|>0.{\rm dim}(E)>\frac{d}{2}\Rightarrow|\Delta(E)|>0.

Here |⋅||\cdot| denotes the Lebesgue measure and dim⁡(⋅){\rm dim}(\cdot) is the Hausdorff dimension.

Following a scheme due to Mattila (c.f. [14, Proposition 2.3]), Theorem 2.3 implies the following result towards Falconer’s conjecture. When d=2,3d=2,3, this recovers the previous best known results of Wolff (d=2, [31]) and D.-Guth-Ou-Wang-Wilson-Z. (d=3, [14]), via a different approach. In the case d≥4d\geq 4, this improves the previous best known result in [14]:

Theorem 2.6.

Let d≥2d\geq 2 and E⊂ℝdE\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set with

Then |Δ⁡(E)|>0|\Delta(E)|>0.

Theorem 2.7.

The rest of this section is devoted to a proof of Proposition 3.1. Note that when the radius R≲1R\lesssim 1, the estimate (3.2) is trivial. So we can assume that RR is sufficiently large compared to any constant depending on ε\varepsilon. We will induct on radius RR in our proof.

In the proof, we will sometimes have paragraphs starting with Intuition. We hope that those could help the readers understand what we do next.

Intuition.

For our union YY of K2K^{2}-cubes, we want to use decoupling theory on each K2K^{2}-cube. This will relate the whole ei​t​Δ​fe^{it\Delta}f to extended functions ei​t​Δ​fτe^{it\Delta}f_{\tau} from various 1/K1/K-caps τ\tau in the frequency space. Instead of doing decoupling in dimension n+1n+1, we are going to do a broad-narrow analysis following Bourgain-Guth [6], Bourgain [3], Bourgain-Demeter [5] and Guth [18]: for each K2K^{2}-cube, one of the two has to happen:

(i) It is broad in the sense that some contributing caps are transversal and form an (n+1)(n+1)-linear structure. In this case the function is controlled by multilinear estimates which are usually strong enough.

(ii) It is narrow (i.e. not broad). In this case all the contributing caps have normal directions close to a hyperplane, which enables us to use decoupling in dimension nn.

Either way we get better estimates than a direct (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional decoupling. We control the broad part directly, and do an induction on the narrow part. Our induction has its roots in the proof of the refined Strichartz estimate in [12, 13].

Throughout this section we fix p=2​(n+1)n−1p=\frac{2(n+1)}{n-1}. In the frequency space we decompose Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1) into disjoint K−1K^{-1}-cubes τ\tau. Denote the set of K−1K^{-1}-cubes τ\tau by 𝒮\mathcal{S}. For function ff with supp​f^⊂Bn​(0,1){\rm supp}\widehat{f}\subset B^{n}(0,1) we have f=∑τfτf=\sum_{\tau}f_{\tau}, where fτ^\widehat{f_{\tau}} is f^\widehat{f} restricted to τ\tau. Given a K2K^{2}-cube BB, we define its significant set

𝒮⁡(B):={τ∈𝒮:‖ei​t​Δ​fτ‖Lp​(B)≥1100​(#​𝒮)​‖ei​t​Δ​f‖Lp​(B)}.\mathcal{S}(B):=\left\{\tau\in\mathcal{S}:\|e^{it\Delta}f_{\tau}\|_{L^{p}(B)}\geq\frac{1}{100(\#\mathcal{S})}\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{p}(B)}\right\}\,.

Note that

‖∑τ∈𝒮⁡(B)ei​t​Δ​fτ‖Lp​(B)∼‖ei​t​Δ​f‖Lp​(B).\big\|\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{S}(B)}e^{it\Delta}f_{\tau}\big\|_{L^{p}(B)}\sim\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{p}(B)}\,.

We say a K2K^{2}-cube BB is narrow if there is an nn-dimensional subspace VV such that for all τ∈𝒮⁡(B)\tau\in\mathcal{S}(B)

Angle⁡(G⁡(τ),V)≤1100​n​K,{\rm Angle}(G(\tau),V)\leq\frac{1}{100nK}\,,

where G⁡(τ)⊂SnG(\tau)\subset S^{n} is a spherical cap of radius ∼K−1\sim K^{-1} given by

G⁡(τ):={(−2​ξ,1)|(−2​ξ,1)|∈Sn:ξ∈τ},G(\tau):=\left\{\frac{(-2\xi,1)}{|(-2\xi,1)|}\in S^{n}:\xi\in\tau\right\}\,,

and Angle⁡(G⁡(τ),V){\rm Angle}(G(\tau),V) denotes the smallest angle between any non-zero vector v∈Vv\in V and v′∈G⁡(τ)v^{\prime}\in G(\tau). Otherwise we say the K2K^{2}-cube BB is broad. It follows from this definition that for any broad BB, there exist τ1,⋯τn+1∈𝒮(B)\tau_{1},\cdots\tau_{n+1}\in\mathcal{S}(B) such that for any vj∈G⁡(τj)v_{j}\in G(\tau_{j})

(3.4) |v1∧v2∧⋯∧vn+1|≳K−n.|v_{1}\wedge v_{2}\wedge\cdots\wedge v_{n+1}|\gtrsim K^{-n}\,.

Denote the union of broad K2K^{2}-cubes BkB_{k} in YY by YbroadY_{\rm broad}, and the union of narrow K2K^{2}-cubes BkB_{k} in YY by YnarrowY_{\rm narrow}. We call it the broad case if YbroadY_{\rm broad} contains ≥M/2\geq M/2 many K2K^{2}-cubes, the narrow case otherwise. We will deal with the broad case in Subsection 3.1 using multilinear refined Strichartz estimate from [13]. And we handle the narrow case in Subsection 3.2 by an inductive argument via the Bourgain-Demeter l2l^{2} decoupling theorem [5] and induction on scales.

3.1. Broad case

Recall that K=RδK=R^{\delta}. A key tool we are using in the broad case is the following multilinear refined Strichartz estimate from [13], which is proved using l2l^{2} decoupling, induction on scales and multilinear Kakeya estimates (see [1, 16]).

Theorem 3.2 (c.f. Theorem 4.2 in [13]).

Let q=2​(n+2)nq=\frac{2(n+2)}{n}. Let ff be a function with Fourier support in Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1). Suppose that τ1,⋯,τn+1∈𝒮\tau_{1},\cdots,\tau_{n+1}\in\mathcal{S} and (3.4) holds for any vj∈G⁡(τj)v_{j}\in G(\tau_{j}). Suppose that Q1,Q2,⋯,QNQ_{1},Q_{2},\cdots,Q_{N} are lattice R1/2R^{1/2}-cubes in BRn+1B_{R}^{n+1}, so that

‖ei​t​Δ​fτi‖Lq​(Qj)​ is dyadically a constant in j, for each i=1,2,⋯,n+1.\|e^{it\Delta}f_{\tau_{i}}\|_{L^{q}(Q_{j})}\textrm{ is dyadically a constant in $j$, for each $i=1,2,\cdots,n+1$}.

Let YY denote ⋃j=1NQj\bigcup_{j=1}^{N}Q_{j}. Then for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

(3.5) ‖∏i=1n+1|ei​t​Δ​fτi|1n+1‖Lq​(Y)≤Cε​Rε​N−n(n+1)​(n+2)​‖f‖2.\left\|\prod_{i=1}^{n+1}\left|e^{it\Delta}f_{\tau_{i}}\right|^{\frac{1}{n+1}}\right\|_{L^{q}(Y)}\leq C_{\varepsilon}R^{\varepsilon}N^{-\frac{n}{(n+1)(n+2)}}\|f\|_{2}\,.

In the broad case, there are ∼M\sim M many broad K2K^{2}-cubes BB. Denote the collection of (n+1)(n+1)-tuple of transverse caps by Γ\Gamma:

Γ:={τ~=(τ1,⋯,τn+1):τj∈𝒮​ and (3.4) holds for any ​vj∈G⁡(τj)}.\Gamma:=\left\{\tilde{\tau}=(\tau_{1},\cdots,\tau_{n+1}):\tau_{j}\in\mathcal{S}\text{ and }\eqref{eq-trans}\text{ holds for any }v_{j}\in G(\tau_{j})\right\}\,.

Then for each broad BB,

(3.6) ‖ei​t​Δ​f‖Lp​(B)p≤KO⁡(1)​∏j=1n+1(∫B|ei​t​Δ​fτj|p)1n+1,\left\|e^{it\Delta}f\right\|^{p}_{L^{p}(B)}\leq K^{O(1)}\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\left(\int_{B}\big|e^{it\Delta}f_{\tau_{j}}\big|^{p}\right)^{\frac{1}{n+1}}\,,

for some τ~=(τ1,⋯,τn+1)∈Γ\tilde{\tau}=(\tau_{1},\cdots,\tau_{n+1})\in\Gamma. In order to exploit the transversality, we want to bound the above geometric average of integrals by an integral of geometric average up to a loss of KO⁡(1)K^{O(1)}. 3.2. Narrow case

For each narrow ball, we have the following lemma which is a consequence of l2l^{2} decoupling theorem in dimension nn and Minkowski’s inequality. This argument is essentially contained in Bourgain-Demeter’s proof of the l2l^{2} decoupling conjecture and we omit the details (see the proof of Proposition 5.5 in [5]).

Lemma 3.3.

Suppose that BB is a narrow K2K^{2}-cube in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. Then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

‖ei​t​Δ​f‖Lp​(B)≤Cε​Kε​(∑τ∈𝒮‖ei​t​Δ​fτ‖Lp​(ωB)2)1/2,\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^{p}(B)}\leq C_{\varepsilon}K^{\varepsilon}\left(\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{S}}\left\|e^{it\Delta}f_{\tau}\right\|_{L^{p}(\omega_{B})}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\,,

here p=2​(n+1)n−1p=\frac{2(n+1)}{n-1}, 𝒮\mathcal{S} denotes the set of K−1K^{-1}-cubes which tile Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1), and ωB\omega_{B} is a weight function which is essentially a characteristic function on BB.

For each τ∈𝒮\tau\in\mathcal{S}, we will deal with ei​t​Δ​fτe^{it\Delta}f_{\tau} by parabolic rescaling and induction on radius. In order to do so, we need to further decompose ff in physical space and perform dyadic pigeonholing several times to get the right picture for our inductive hypothesis at scale R1:=R/K2R_{1}:=R/K^{2} after rescaling.

Intuition.

For each 1/K1/K-cap τ\tau, all wave packets associated with fτf_{\tau} through a given point have to lie in a common box that has one side length RR and other side lengths R/KR/K. Every single box of this type will become an R/K2R/K^{2}-ball if we perform a parabolic rescaling to transform τ\tau into the standard 11-cap. We want to use the inductive hypothesis for radius R/K2R/K^{2} in an efficient way. A bunch of dyadic pigeonholing steps will be needed.

First, we break the physical ball Bn​(0,R)B^{n}(0,R) into R/KR/K-cubes DD. Intuition.

To finish our inductive argument, we have to relate the old and new parameters. Our setup allows ourselves to do this in a nice way: Given M1,λ1M_{1},\lambda_{1} and γ1\gamma_{1}, if η\eta is small, i.e. each SS contains very few narrow K2K^{2}-cubes, then MM is relatively small; if η\eta is large, i.e. each SS contains a lot of narrow K2K^{2}-cubes, then λ\lambda and γ\gamma are relatively large. Both make the RHS of what we want to prove reasonably large. This is the reason why one could believe the numerology will work out.

Consider the cardinality of the set {(□,B):□∈𝔹,B⊂Y□∩Y′}\{(\Box,B):\Box\in\mathbb{B},B\subset Y_{\Box}\cap Y^{\prime}\}. By our choice of μ\mu as in (3.16), there is a lower bound

#{(□,B):□∈𝔹,B⊂Y□∩Y′}≳(logR)−7Mμ.\#\{(\Box,B):\Box\in\mathbb{B},B\subset Y_{\Box}\cap Y^{\prime}\}\gtrsim(\log R)^{-7}M\mu\,.

On the other hand, by our choices of M1M_{1} and η\eta, for each □∈𝔹\Box\in\mathbb{B}, Y□Y_{\Box} contains ∼M1\sim M_{1} tubes SS and each SS contains ∼η\sim\eta narrow cubes in YnarrowY_{\rm narrow}, so

#{(□,B):□∈𝔹,B⊂Y□∩Y′}≲(#𝔹)M1η.\#\{(\Box,B):\Box\in\mathbb{B},B\subset Y_{\Box}\cap Y^{\prime}\}\lesssim(\#\mathbb{B})M_{1}\eta\,.

Therefore, we get

3.3. Remark

In Section 2, we have seen that Corollary 1.6 is a direct result of Theorem 1.5, and they are equally useful in applications to the sharp L2L^{2} estimate of Schrödinger maximal function. We can also prove Corollary 1.6 from scratch using a similar argument as in this section, which is slightly easier in two aspects compared to that of Theorem 1.5. First, in the broad case, it is sufficient to use multilinear restriction estimates and not necessary to invoke multilinear refined Strichartz. Secondly, because there is one parameter less, the dyadic pigeonholing argument in the narrow case would be slightly reduced, for example, see Figure 2 for tubes of different scales in the □\Box under the setting of Corollary 1.6.

In fact, an adaptation of some arguments in the work [31] of Wolff on the Falconer distance set problem in dimension 22 can already imply Corollary 1.6 when n=1n=1. In the special case n=1n=1, the broad versus narrow dichotomy becomes the one on bilinear versus linear. To handle the linear part, the idea of induction on scales and splitting the ball into rectangular boxes “□\Box” of size R×R/KR\times R/K in our proof already existed in Wolff’s paper. We thank Hong Wang for pointing this out to us and sharing some notes on it.
